title: Mahender Singh vs Mukesh Kumar on 9 July, 2024
full_text: Mahender Singh vs Mukesh Kumar on 9 July, 2024 IN THE COURT OF MS. VINERJEET KAUR MM (N.I. ACT-03) SOUTH-WEST: DWARKA COURTS: NEW DELHI CNR No.DLSW02-001951-2020 Ct. Case No.1468/2020 U/s.138 N.I. Act . MAHENDER SINGH VS. MUKESH KUMAR Date of Institution of case: 13.01.2020 Date of which Judgment reserved: 04.07.2024. Date on which judgment pronounced: 09.07.2024. JUDGMENT 1) Unique ID no. of the case : CNR No.DLSW02-001951-2020 2) Name of complainant : Mahender Singh, S/o Late Sh. Shyam Lal R/o House No. 98/31, Mahalaxmi Garden, Gali No.5, Rajendra Park, Gurgaon, Haryana. 3) Name and address of accused : Mukesh Kumar S/o Jai Prakash Singh R/o House No. G-1/113, New Palam Vihar, Phase-II, Gurgaon, Haryana-122017. 4) Offence complained of : Section 138 N.I. Act 5) Plea of accused : Accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 1/21 6) Final Order : Acquitted for the offence punishable U/s.138 N.I. Act 7) Date of order : 09.07.2024 BRIEF STATEMENT OF REASONS FOR THE DECISION:- 1. The present complaint has been filed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter " NI Act ") by Mahender Singh (hereinafter "complainant") against Mukesh Kumar (hereinafter "accused"). 2. The substance of allegations, as contained in the complaint, are as follows: A. That the accused is a relative of the complainant and had good friendly relation with him. The accused borrowed an amount of Rs.51,750/- in cash from the complainant in the month of July, 2019. Despite repeated demands of the complainant, the accused failed to repay the aforesaid borrowed amount to the complainant within agreed period on one pretext or another. B. On repeated demands of the complainant, the accused towards the repayment of the aforesaid borrowed amount as well as towards the discharge of his legal liability, issued a cheque in favour of complainant i.e. cheque bearing No. 000012 dated 26.11.2019 for an amount of Rs.51,750/- drawn on HDFC Bank Ltd., Palam Vihar, Grameen Bank, Gurugram, Haryana. C. That the complainant has presented this cheque for encashment with his banker but the said cheque was received back unpaid with the remarks "Payment Stopped by the Drawer" vide cheque return memo dated 26.11.2019. Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 2/21 D. That thereafter, the complainant sent the accused a legal notice dated 11.12.2019 through his counsel. 3. Accused's stance, on the contrary, at the stage of framing of notice under section 251 CrPC was that complainant is his uncle from his maternal side and they had stayed together for around an year. Post that one of his cheques went missing, thus he stopped payment via internet banking. He further stated that he did not know as to how the cheque came into the possession of the complainant. He stated that the complainant had stolen his cheque and has filed a false and frivolous complaint against him. Further, he submitted that he did not owe any liability towards the complainant. 4. Pre-summoning evidence was led by the complainant and on finding a prima facie case, the accused was summoned to face trial. On appearance, the accused was served with the notice of accusation under Section 251 , Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter " CrPC "), to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The accused was granted an opportunity to cross-examine the complainant. 5. During the trial, the complainant led the following oral and documentary evidence against the accused to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt:- Oral Evidence CW-1/A Testimony of complainant Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 3/21 Documentary Evidence Ex. CW1/1 Cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 Cheque Return Memo Ex.CW1/3 Legal notice Ex.CW1/4 Postal receipt Ex.CW1/5 Aadhar Card 6. Thereafter, before the start of defence evidence, in order to allow the accused to personally explain the circumstances appearing in evidence against him, his statement under Section 313 CrPC was recorded without oath. In reply, the accused submitted the following in his statement under section 313 CrPC: ● He stated that the complainant is a near relative of his but he had never borrowed any money from him. Rather it is the complainant who had borrowed money from him during the marriage ceremony of the accused's sister. The accused had lent Rs.30,000/- to the complainant and he got the same transferred from the bank account of his friend namely Prakash to the bank account of the complainant. This happened twice or thrice. ● He also stated that the complainant used to travel with him in his car where his cheques were lying and might have stolen the cheque in question from his car. When, he asked the complainant to repay the amount that he had lent him, he avoided returning the same on various pretexts. Dishonour of cheque is a matter of record. He further stated that complainant has misused the cheque in question. Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 4/21 ● The accused further denied receiving the legal notice sent by the complainant. The accused took the same stance as in his defence while framing notice under Section 251 CrPC. 7. The accused opted to lead defence evidence during the statement under Section 313 CrPC, and he examined as DW-1 Sh. Jai Parkash, DW-2 Sh. Prakash Kumar and DW-3 Sh. Susheel Sagar. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After listening to final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement. I have heard the learned counsels on both the sides and have given my thoughtful consideration to the material appearing on record. 9. Before appreciation of evidence led on behalf of the parties, at the very outset, I would like to narrate the legal principles, relevant for adjudication of complaint under Section 138 of NI Act. 10. Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes dishonour of cheques an offence. It provides that: "where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 5/21 of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both". 11. In order to ascertain whether the accused has committed an offence u/s 138 NI Act, the following ingredients constituting the offence have to be proved: (i) The drawer of the cheque should have issued the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. (ii) The cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank. (iii) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days of the receipt of the notice from the payee or the holder in due course demanding the payment of the said amount of money. It is only when all the above-mentioned ingredients are satisfied that the person Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 6/21 who has drawn the cheque can be said to have committed an offence u/s 138 NI Act. 12. It is important to reproduce Sec.118 and Sec.139 of the NI Act here. Section 118 (a) of the NI Act provides that: "until the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that "that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration." Further, Section 139 of the NI Act lays down that: "it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 13. The combined effect of section 118(a) NI Act and section 139 of the NI Act is that a presumption exists that the cheque was drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability. In Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16), their Lordships of Hon'ble Supreme Court observed as follows: Because both Sections 138 and 139 require that the Court "shall presume" the liability of the drawer of the cheques for the amounts Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 7/21 for which the cheques are drawn, as noted in State of Madras vs. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer AIR 1958 SC 61, it is obligatory on the Court to raise this presumption in every case where the factual basis for the raising of the presumption had been established. "It introduces an exception to the general rule as to the burden of proof in criminal cases and shifts the onus on to the accused" (ibid). Such a presumption is a presumption of law, as distinguished from a presumption of fact which describes provisions by which the court "may presume" a certain state of affairs. Presumptions are rules of evidence and do not conflict with the presumption of innocence, because by the latter all that is meant is that the prosecution is obliged to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt. In this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court, having analysed all the concerned provisions in Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418 : 2019 SCC OnLine SC 491 at page 432, came down to the following conclusion: "25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of theAct mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 8/21 discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. 25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." 14. In this case, issuance of cheque, its presentation and dishonouring are not in dispute, inasmuch as the same have been duly proved on the basis of cogent evidence as well as admitted by the accused. The signature on the cheque in question Ex.CW1/1 has been denied by the accused and the burden to prove this fact was on the accused Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 9/21 and he has failed to discharge the burden. He could have called a bank witness to prove that the signatures on the cheque do not match his signatures. He could have proved that the signatures were not his by proving a document which had his signatures and shown that the signatures on the cheque were different than his proven signatures. His failure to prove that the signatures on the cheque were not his, leads the court to believe that the cheque in question was indeed signed by him. The aforesaid cheque in question was returned unpaid vide return memo bearing Ex.CW1/2. The legal notice bearing Ex.CW1/3 was sent to the accused vide postal receipt bearing Ex.CW1/4. No tracking report was filed. As far as the receipt of legal demand notice is concerned, I shall discuss the same at a later stage of this judgments. 15. In view of the above-mentioned circumstances, the presumptions under sections 139 and 118 NI Act that the cheque in question was for a legally recoverable debt/liability stand activated. 16. Simply stated, the accused has to offer on something that makes his version probable. This the accused can do by both successfully raising and proving competing version to the case of the complainant or by perforating the case of the complainant. Opportunity to do this arises for the accused at four stages: - (i) When the accused puts forth defence at the time when his plea of defence as recorded after the substance of acquisition explained to him u/s 251 CrPC Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 10/21 (ii) When the accused cross examines the complainant pursuant to his application u/S.145(2) N.I. Act being allowed. (iii) When statement of the accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC and (iv) When defence witness was examined. The stand taken by the accused at all these stages shall be examined to determine if the accused could raise a probable defence. 17. It is evident that the onus was on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption. Therefore, the accused was required to bring on record such facts and circumstances, which would make the court believe that he had not issued the cheque in question as alleged and that the complainant had misused his cheque. 18. The argument raised by the accused is that the complainant is a relative of his and had lived with him for around an year. Further they used to travel together, and some of his cheques were lying in his car. He stated that the complainant might have stolen the cheque in question from there. He stated that he had not borrowed any money from the complainant, but on the contrary he had lent him some money which he had got transferred through one Prakash Kumar. He has examined this Prakash Kumar as DW2 and he has deposed that he transferred some money into the account of the complainant because the accused asked him to do so. His defence is that the complainant must have stolen his cheque and later used it to file the present complaint. He has raised various points to show that the complaint is not maintainable and further Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 11/21 that he does not owe any legal liability to the complainant. 19. The first objection raised on behalf of the accused is that the offence under section 138 NI Act, 1881 is not made out as the legal notice dated 11.12.2019 was not served upon him. In fact, no tracking report has been filed by the complainant. He further states that even the address mentioned on the legal notice is not his correct address. In fact, the address given by the accused during the framing of the notice against him and again during his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C is different than the address mentioned on the legal notice. Thereafter the burden to prove that the address mentioned on the legal notice was the correct address of the accused was on the complainant. However, the complainant could not prove that the address on the legal notice was that of the accused. It is not even the case that the summons were served on the same address. The complainant during his cross-examination at the stage of complainant's evidence has admitted that he had given a fresh address to the court when the summons issued by the court were not served on the address given initially. To constitute an offence under Section 138 NI Act, sending or giving of legal demand notice is not enough, it is the 'receipt of notice' by the drawer or his agent that is critical. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan & Anr , The Supreme Court held that, failure on the part of the drawer to pay the amount should be within 15 days 'of the receipt of the said notice. It is, therefore, clear that 'giving notice' in the context is not akin to 'receipt of notice'. It is duty of payee to send the notice to the correct address. In D. Vinod Shivappa v. Nanda Belliappa , the question before the Court was Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 12/21 whether in a case where the postal endorsement showed that the notice could not be served on account of the non availability of the addressee, a cause of action could still arise for prosecution of the drawer of the cheque on the basis of deemed service of notice under clause (c) of proviso to Section 138 NI Act. The Court held that, this question had to be answered by reference to the facts of each case and no rule of universal application could be laid down that in all cases where notice was not served on account of non-availability of the addressee, the Court must presume service of notice. It elaborated as follows--"If a notice is issued and served upon the drawer of the cheque, no controversy arises. Similarly if the notice is refused by the addressee, it may be presumed to have been served. This is also not disputed. This leaves us with the third situation where the notice could not be served on the addressee for one or the other reason, such as his non availability at the time of delivery, or premises remaining locked on account of his having gone elsewhere etc. If in each such case the law is understood to mean that there has been no service of notice, it would completely defeat the very purpose of the Act. It would then be very easy for an unscrupulous and dishonest drawer of a cheque to make himself scarce for sometime after issuing the cheque so that the requisite statutory notice can never be served upon him and consequently he can never be prosecuted. There is good authority to support the proposition that once the complainant, the payee of the cheque, issues notice to the drawer of the cheque, the cause of action to file a complaint arises on the expiry of the period prescribed for payment by the drawer of the cheque. If the complainant is able to prove that the drawer of the cheque knew about the notice and deliberately evaded Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 13/21 service and got a false endorsement made only to defeat the process of law, the Court shall presume service of notice. This, however, is a matter of evidence and proof. Thus even in a case where the notice is returned with the endorsement that the premises has always been found locked or the addressee was not available at the time of postal delivery, it will be open to the complainant to prove at the trial by evidence that the endorsement is not correct and that the addressee, namely the drawer of the cheque, with knowledge of the notice had deliberately avoided to receive notice. The question as to whether the service of notice has been fraudulently refused by unscrupulous means is a question of fact to be decided on the basis of evidence ". The Apex Court reiterated in Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. v. M/s Galaxy Traders that, it is not the 'giving' of the notice which makes the offence but it is the 'receipt' of the notice and non payment thereafter, by the drawer which gives the cause of action to the complainant to file the complaint within the statutory period. The Hon'ble HC of Delhi in R L Varma and Sons (HUF) v PC Sharma, CRL. REV. P. 438/2017 held that when notice is sent at the wrong address, the presumption of service under section 27 of GCA r/w section 114 of Indian Evidence Act ( hereinafter IEA) does not apply. It was held that, Legal presumption of service of notice can only arise in case the notice is correctly addressed. If the notice is incorrectly addressed no legal presumption can arise. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act mandates the issuance of the statutory notice as a pre-condition to filing of a complaint. The cause of action to file a complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act arises only on issuance and service of statutory notice and failure of the accused to Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 14/21 comply with the statutory notice. In the absence of service of statutory notice the cause of action would not accrue. Service of statutory notice would also include legal presumption of service if circumstances so warrant. As a legal notice was incorrectly addressed and consequently, there was no service on the accused, the legal notice will not be deemed to have been served and therefore the offence under section 138 of negotiable instruments act is not made out. 20. The next argument raised by the accused is that despite being asked to produce any document or account of the business from which the complainant had withdrawn the money to give to the accused, the complainant had failed to do so. Accused has argued that this goes to show that the complainant never withdrew any money as alleged by him, and consequently, never gave any money to the accused. The complainant in his cross-examination has stated that he gave the sum of ₹51,750/- to the accused in cash in the denomination of ₹500/- and some change. He also stated that he had not lent any money to one Prakash Kumar. The complainant was confronted with the statement of bank account of Prakash Kumar, Exhibit CW1/DX1, wherein his attention was drawn to certain entries which reflected the transfer of money from the account of Prakash Kumar to his account. To this, he first answered that this was the money that he had given to Prakash Kumar in cash, and he had transferred it in his account for the instalments qua the payment of loan for the truck debited from his account. However, he also volunteered that he was confused as to why there were these entries showing the transfer from the account of Prakash Kumar Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 15/21 to his account. At the stage of defence evidence, this Prakash Kumar was summoned as a witness. In his testimony, he deposed that he did not know the complainant and had transferred the money into the account of the complainant because the accused asked him to do so, and he had got the same amount in cash from the accused. During the cross-examination of the said witness, his credibility or the credibility of his testimony could not be impeached. These points do raise reasonable doubt about the genuineness of the complainant case and point towards a probable defence. 21. In continuation of his argument, the accused has also pointed out that as per the complainant, the cheque in question was given at the house of the complainant, in the presence of the father of the accused and the family members of the complainant, including his wife. The complainant has not examined any of the witnesses regarding the receipt of the cheque from the accused. This evidence would have been material specially considering the defence taken by the accused. If the complainant had brought some evidence to show that the accused had himself given him the cheque, it would have been the best rebuttal to the assertion of the accused that the cheque had been stolen from him. However, the accused has examined his father as DW1 and DW1 has deposed that he does not know anything about the complainant giving any money to the accused. The witness was not cross examined despite being given a chance to do so. These facts also do not favour the case of the complainant. The counsel for the accused has also argued that during his cross-examination, the complainant has stated that he got the cheque from the accused on 26 November 2019, and that he presented it Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 16/21 on the same date. He argues that as per the complainant he got the cheque in the afternoon and it is unlikely that he would have presented it that very day. This argument does not hold much merit as it is common knowledge that the banks are open till evening, and it is likely that a person will present the cheque on the same date when he receives it. 22. The accused also examined a bank witness from HDFC bank. He brought on record a document which is exhibit CW1/DX2 and as per the document the accused had issued an instruction on 11/11/2019 at 10:42:09 through internet banking, that the payment to cheque number 000012 was to be stopped. As per the complainant, the cheque was issued to him on 26/11/2019. It seems improbable that the accused would first issue a stop payment instruction on a cheque and then issued the same cheque to a person in discharge of some liability. The reason for the stop payment instruction has not been given by the accused. However, during the trial, he had explained that when he found out that his cheque was missing, he issued the said instruction. Now the burden was on the complainant to prove that this instruction had been issued maliciously. 23. The counsel for the accused has also argued that three different pens have been used on the cheque in question. During his cross-examination, the complainant had first stated that the cheque in question was given fully filled up and then stated that it was filled up in his presence. When he was cross examined on this point on another Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 17/21 date, he answered that the accused had filled in the particular except the name of the payee and the date which were filled by him. These contradictions by the complainant do not work in his favour. Another point which has been stressed upon by the counsel for the accused is that in the evidence affidavit and the complaint at para number 5 and 4 respectively, the cheque number has been incorrectly written as 324577 dated 15 November 2019. The complainant was asked about this during his cross examination, but he failed to offer any clarification. Even if the court is to consider that this might have been a typographical error, it was the duty of the complainant to offer a clarification, and he has failed to do so. The accused has also argued that the amount in the cheque is too specific and does not appear to be genuine. However this argument is not sustainable and is thus being rejected. Although these points do not hold much weightage when seen individually, cumulatively, they tend to add to the scale, which is already leaning in favour of the accused. 24. The accused was required to prove his case on the touchstone of benchmark set in the judgment as held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kumar Exports vs Sharma Carpets (2009)2 SCC 513, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court had held as follows: "The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the nonexistence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 18/21 consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the nonexistence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not served the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their nonexistence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on to the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 19/21 presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act. The accused has also an option to prove the nonexistence of consideration and debt or liability either by letting in evidence or in some clear and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial. Once such rebuttal evidence is adduced and accepted by the court, having regard to all the circumstances of the case and the preponderance of probabilities, the evidentiali burden shifts back to the complainant and, thereafter, the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act will not again come to the complainant's rescue." 25. Since the accused has discharged the burden it was the complainant who has to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt. The complainant has failed to do so and therefore despite few inconsistencies, the benefit goes to the accused. 26. Since the accused has discharged the burden it was the complainant who has to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt. The complainant has failed to do so and therefore despite few inconsistencies, the benefit goes to the accused. 27. To recapitulate the above discussion, the complainant has been unsuccessful in establishing his case beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of his legally enforceable liability. The presumptions under Section 118 and Section 139 of N.I. Act have been successfully rebutted. The accused has been able to raise a probable defence. The defence of the accused that the complainant misused the cheque in question and there was no legal liability of Rs. Ct. Case No. 1468/2020 Mahender Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar 20/21 51,750/- is proved on the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 28. Resultantly, the complaint of the complainant is dismissed, and the accused Mukesh Kumar, is hereby acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
